title: Big Trouble
full_review:
Touchstone already had a lame loser on its hands with the ensemble comedy "Big Trouble," but after September 11 the studio should have not just postponed its premiere. Chalking it up as unreleasable would have been a wiser course of action.

Six months may have passed since the attacks, but just when would a plot be considered hilarious that has criminals without any identification allowed to board a commercial jetliner with a trunk containing a large nuclear device about to detonate?

And that explosive climax concludes a failed screwball comedy populated by characters either shrill or flat, chasing one another through unfunny situations while uttering witless dialogue.

The set-up is based on popular humorist Dave Barry's novel of the same name. A divorced dad (Tim Allen) and his teen son (Ben Foster) become involved with the Herk family -- thieving dad (Stanley Tucci), unhappy mom (Rene Russo) and teen daughter (Zooey Deschanel). Hitmen (including Dennis Farina) have been sent to rub out dad but other characters get in the way, such as dopey ex-cons (including Tom Sizemore), cops (including Janeane Garofalo), FBI agents (including Omar Epps), a maid (Sofia Vergara), a hippy (Jason Lee) and Russian arms dealers. There are mindless chase scenes, abrasive confrontations and chatter delivered in deadpan style that is already d.o.a. And who knows what else may have been cut from the rather short running time (though not short enough) since the choppy editing leads one to believe something is amiss in what director Barry Sonnenfeld hoped would be a madcap comedy.

Instead it looks like a film dictated by youth demographics: throw in several teen-agers, a sexy maid, supposedly macho guys with weapons and fast cars and tough talking one-liners, and surely a hit will materialize.

Hope it misses big time or big trouble is what movie lovers will increasingly find as they look for intelligent, entertaining cinema.

Due to much profanity, some violence, brief sexual situations, rear nudity, double entendres and crass expressions, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
